 Vs.

full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J.—This appeal arises from First Miscellaneous Appeal No.98 of 1984 decided by a Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka (Mr. Justice Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury & Mr. Justice Amin-ur-Rahman Khan) on 22nd August 1984 dismissing the appeal preferred by the appellants against an order of injunction and attachment passes by the District Judge, Dhaka on 27.3.84 in miscellaneous Case No. 117 of 1983 under Article 33 of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 (President’s Order No. 128 of 1972). 

 2. fact are; Respondent No. 1, namely Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, hereinafter called the Sangstha instituted the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 117 of 1983, in the Court of District Judge Dhaka against the appellants and respondent Nos. 2-5 stating that on the prayer of Tapashes Shipping Lines Ltd. (respondent No. 2), respondent No.1 sanctioned the loan of Tk. 70,00,000/- on 31st March 1980 in favour of respondent No. 2 for acquisition of two 600 DWT Cargo vessels. Estimated cost for the project is Tk. 117 lacs, Respondent No. 2 approached Dira Dockyard and Engineers Ltd. appellant No.1 for construction of the above mentioned cargo vessels. On 28th  September 1980 a tripartite contract was made between appellant No. 1, respondent No. 1 and respondent No.2 According to the terms of the contract as quoted below  appellant No.1 undertook to contract two vessels. The contract is as follows: 

 ARTICLE: 2 Price of one number steel body. (self propelled) cargo coaster of capacity 600 DWT complete as per specifications and approved plan/design is Tk. 47,87,500/- (Taka forty seven lacs eighty seven thousand and five hundred) only. The total price of the 2 (two) coasters is Tk. 95,75,000/-. Out of this, amount BSRS will pay Tk. 70,00,000/- only by establishment of an irrevocable letter of credit and the balance Tk. 25,75,000/- only will be paid by them through a crossed cheque on a scheduled bank. The builder shall never in-crease the price of the coasters from toe quoted amount in any case. 

 ARTICLE 5. The coasters will be delivered within 6-8 month, from the date of the disbursement of the 1st installment a, per schedule of payment detailed to in Article 3. In case of failure to deliver the coaster within the schedule time the builder shall be liable to pay the Purchaser a compensation @ Tk. 1000/- (Taka one thousand) only per coaster per day for the period of such default. 

 ARTICLE 6. Before delivery, the builder undertakes to submit a performance guarantee in form and substance prescribed by BSRS amounting to 5% or the total value of the coasters from Shadharan Bima Corporation which shall remain valid as least 1 (one) year from the date of delivery of the Coasters. In case the builder fails to deliver the coaster within 5-8  months, the builder shall extend the validity of the Insurance, guarantee suitably so as to fulfill the above conditions. 

 3. In pursuance of this contract an amount of Tk. 14,00,000/- was paid to appellant No.1 on 4th November 1980 About B month thereafter, that is, on 6th December 1980 Tk. 28,000,00/- was also paid towards the costs of construction of the vessels. In violation of the terms of contract and the letter of credit appellant No.1 imported two second hand, re-reconditioned and used marine engines. Further though according to terms of the contract, the vessels should have been completed/delivered by 16th December 1981 using new steel plates and fitted with new Kalvin marine diesel engines neither such completion nor delivery was made. As a result of the violations of the contract by appellant No. 1, dispute arose between it and the Sangstha. Respondent No. 1. served a nonce under Article 32 of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order (President’s Order No.128 of 1972) upon them but having received no reply respondent No. 1 filed an application under Article 33 of the aforesaid Presidential Order. Respondent No. 1 filed all application for injunction and attachment before judgment which the learned District Judge granted on 27th March 1984, on the finding that the Sangstha had a strong prima facie case against the appellants as well as respondent Nos. 2-6. The learned Judges of the High Court Division on finding that the District Judge was justified in passing the order of injunction as well as  the order attachment affirmed his order in the first miscellaneous appeal being F.M.A. No. 98 of 1984. Preferred by the appellants. 

 7. The case of respondent is that since the amount of Tk. 42,00,000/- was part of the total amount advanced to respondent No. 2, It fell within the definition of the term "loan" in the aforesaid Order and as the appellants received this amount from the Sangstha according to the terms of the tripartite agreement they are also liable to repay it and, In case of this failure to do so, the procedure laid down in Article 33 of the aforesaid Order is applicable to them. According to the tripartite agreement, appellants are involved in the process of disbursement of the loan and received a part of the total loan sanctioned earlier to respondent No. 2 and if the amount of Tk. 42,00,000/- is considered to be a part of the roan transaction between the Sangstha and respondent No. 2, appellants being recipient of the part of such loan are under obligation to repay it. On their failure to discharge the obligation arising from the loan transaction between the Sangstha, Tapaahee Shipping Lines Ltd. and the appellants the summary procedure for realisation of loan advanced to an industrial concern and any person liable for payment of that loan as prescribed in Article 33 of the Order should extend to the latter, namely, the appellants. It may be argued that the loan transaction was entered between the Sangstha and respondent No. 2 but by virtue of the tripartite agreement between the Sangstha, respondent No. 2 and the appellants according to which the appellants had and received a part of the total amount of loan, they rendered themselves liable to repay the loan and on their refusal to do it the Sangstha may take recourse to Article 33. 

 11. It is true, as was submitted by the appellant's learned Counsel, that the amount of Tk. 42,00,000/- paid to his clients for construction of the vessels cannot be termed as either guarantee or indemnity", as included In the definition of loan. Is may, however, be examined whether "any liability which the Sangstha may Incur on behalf of an industrial concern" as occurs in the same definition can be applied to the aforesaid amount so that the same may be treated as loan by the Sangstha to the appellants. In my view the aforesaid amount paid by the Sangstha to the appellants for the purposes mentioned in the agreement is a liability which has been incurred by the Sangstha on account of respondent No. 2 and the reason for saying so is that since the agreement is between the Sangstha and the appellants and the amount paid to the appellants by the Sangstha comes from and forms part of the loan Venice to respondent No. 2, in case of failure to fulfill the agreement by the appellants, respondent No. 2 may claim this amount over again from the Sangstha as the Sangstha instead of giving this amount to respondent No. 2 paid it directly to the appellants and consequently respondent No. 2 though granted the loan out of which the amount was paid to the appellants, never had or received this amount float the Sangstha. Quite arguably if this claim is ever made by respondent  No. 2 to the Sangstha they would seem to have a good case. 

 12. In addition to such seemingly accept- able contention, on some critical analysis of the opening words of the tripartite agreement, it would be seen that the agreement with the appellants reveals that the same is between Bangladesh Shilpa Ria Sangstha A/C. M/S. Tapashee Shipping Lines Ltd. Dhaka herein after called the purchaser" and M/T. Dira Dockyard and Engineers Ltd. Shimrail, Demra, Dhaka hereinafter called the "builder" The Sangstha thus entered into the agreement with the appellants on account of respondent No. 2 and instead of paying the entire amount of loan granted to respondent No. 2 gave part of the loan amount, according to the terms and condition of the agreement to the appellants. Why on this ground "lone the amount of Tk. 42,00,000/- which has been given to the appellants, should not fail within the definition of loan? Apparently it may sound nice and acceptable that no loan was granted to the appellants whatever amount was paid to them was towards the price of the vessels agreed to be built by 'he appellants bus in the totality of the context of what preceded, the payment of the amount would conclusively show that the appellants knew and consented to receive this amount on account of the loan granted to respondent No. 2 and the sum paid to them was a pare of the total amount granted to respondent No. 2 The very words used in the agreement, namely, A/C. M/S. Tapashee Shipping Lines Ltd., Dhaka" bear testimony to the context against which Tk. 42,00,000/- was paid to the appellants Judging from this angle also the amount paid to the appellants is or becomes part or the loan. Once the amount so paid to the appellants becomes loan as defined in the Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972  not only respondent  No. 2 to whom the loan was grunted but also the appellants who have received and had part of that loan becomes liable for payment of that loan as mentioned in Article 33(1) of the aforesaid Order. For, this article shows that when there is a breach of any condition of the agreement between the Sangstha and an industrial  concern to which any loan has been granted or any person liable for payment of that loan, the Sangstha may proceed to recover the loan from them according to the procedure laid down in the Article, There is some point in the contention raised by the appellants' counsel that the loan was granted to respondent No. 2 and not the appellants but if it can be established, as has been done in the present case, that some- body else also received part of that loan under some legal arrangements (in this case under tripartite agreement between the Sangstha, respondent No. 2 and the appellants) such person becomes liable for payment of that loan and also amenable to the procedure for recovery of the loan prescribed thereunder. In these facts and circumstances I find no reason to interfere with the order of the learned Judges of the High Court Division though at the same time I do not feel inclined to agree with all the reasons behind the order passed by them. Appellants Counsel, in support of his argument that the amount paid to the appellants was not loan as defined in the aforesaid order, referred to a case decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan namely, Ocean Industries Ltd. Vs. Industrial Development Bank, (1966) 18 DLR (SC) 354; PLD 966 SC 938. In this case the question whether a guarantee provided by the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan for payment of certain installments t, be paid to the foreign  shipbuilder was 'loan" was raised, Section 39(1) of the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan ordinance 1961 provided that 'where an industrial concern fails to repay such loan by the due date or in compliance with the notice under section 38, an officer of the Bank, generally or specially authorised by the Board in this behalf, may apply to the District Judge in 1965 by an amending Ordinance the definition of the term 'loan" was inserted which included a guarantee. This amendment could not, however, be relied on as the decision of the High Court was given before this amendment was made Even so. the Supreme Court concluded that after the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan had in fulfillment of Its guarantee, paid the first two installments to the ship, builders and the insurance premise, upon the failure of the appellant Company to repay the sums, it became entitled to recover the same from the appellant company, an money paid to the use of the principal debtor. According to the Supreme Court, the amount so paid constituted an advance and the relationship of debtor and creditor arose between the surety and the principal debtor. Further, the debt assumed the characteristics of a loan, Reason why the amount co advanced was loan was that this amount had to be repaid, Hamoodur Rahman. J who delivered the judgment of the Supreme Court, observed: 

 13. We do not quite follow how this decision supports the appellants. The only difference between this case and the facts of the instant case before us is that in the former the conditions of repayment were laid down, whereas in she tripartite agreement between the Sangstha and respondent No. 2 on the one hand and the appellants on the other does not mention any mode of repayment, but we are of the vie a that even with-out such mode of repayment of the  amount paid to the appellants being described in the tripartite agreements  when reference to the aforesaid tripartite agreement, it appears that it was entered into on account of respondent No. 2 to whom the loan was granted and the Sangstha in fulfillment of such loan transaction between it and respondent No. 2 paid  part of the amount to the appellants which the appellants received, it follows that they must be said to have fallen within the meaning of the clause "any person liable for payment of that loan". Amounts paid to the appellants can, therefore, be recovered from them according to the summary procedure laid down in Article 33 of the Order.
